query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from high-thermal-load fusion-based additive manufacturing to a binder jetting process followed by moderate-temperature sintering of AlCrFeNiSi powder will reduce residual stress, improve mechanical properties, and simplify processing for miniature components relative to laser powder bed fusion benchmarks.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with particle size distribution suitable for binder jet printing and subsequent sintering.
generation.intervention: Fabricate near-net-shape binder-jetted AlCrFeNiSi parts and then sinter at approximately 1100–1200 °C in an inert or vacuum environment.
generation.conditions: Use a moderate sintering hold time (e.g., 2–4 hours), ensuring uniform heating and slow cooling to minimize internal stress. Print and sinter small-scale components (e.g., <10 mm in thickness).
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients and microstructural coarsening during the post-print sintering cycle compared to the rapid heating/cooling of laser or electron beam processes.
generation.mechanism: Eliminating high thermal gradients inherent to fusion-based AM prevents the buildup of residual stresses, while controlled sintering promotes diffusion-driven densification and uniform microstructure formation, leading to more consistent mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to laser powder bed fusion parts, binder-jetted and sintered components will exhibit significantly lower residual stresses, improved microstructural homogeneity, and comparable or better strength and ductility in small-scale testing, while reducing process complexity.
generation.baseline: Conventional laser-based metal additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi under typical high-thermal-load conditions (e.g., laser power >200 W, rapid solidification).
generation.boundary: Applies to AlCrFeNiSi powder suited for binder jetting processes with moderate heating profiles during sintering; may require design modifications to address shrinkage and ensure net shape in miniature components.
generation.uncertainty: Exact mechanical property improvements and dimensional accuracies need to be experimentally verified. The degree of shrinkage and phase evolution during sintering requires optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce identical miniaturized AlCrFeNiSi test coupons by binder jetting plus sintering and compare them against laser powder bed fused counterparts of the same geometry. Quantify residual stresses by X-ray diffraction, measure hardness and tensile strength, then compare fabrication complexity and resultant microstructures.
measurements: Optical microscopy and SEM for microstructural homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the residual stresses, mechanical properties, or production complexity of the binder-jetted and sintered samples do not outperform or match those made with laser powder bed fusion, the hypothesis is invalidated.

Apart from the currently dominating laser- and electron-beam based AM methods, alternative methods to metal AM have been developed, such as binder jetting and 3D ink-extrusion printing where first a binder-containing green body is shaped at ambient temperature from elemental or pre-alloyed powders that is then densified in a subsequent isothermal sintering step. These techniques have the potential to provide segregation-free, structurally-homogeneous alloys with low residual stress due to full inter-diffusion and isothermal sintering, while also reducing cost and eliminating the need of inert-gas processing environments of beam-based AM. The inks for 3D ink-extrusion can be produced from alloyed metal powder, elemental powder or compounds that reduce (e.g., oxides) or decompose (e.g., hydrides) to metal upon thermal processing. The elimination of pre-alloying steps (i.e., to create powders for selective laser melting) and the ability to directly produce alloys from blended pure oxide feedstock further reduce cost, time, and provide full flexibility of alloy composition. Many scholars have studied HEAs [,,], but most focus on design principles, metallurgical mechanisms, phase changes, micro-structures, and properties of HEAs manufactured by conventional technologies. Several AM methods have been successfully implemented to fabricate structures with HEAs []. The powder bed fusion (PBF) processes, specifically the selected laser melting (SLM) technique, have been widely adopted []. SLM is a powder-bed additive manufacturing technology, which is also advantageous for producing complex-shaped parts []. During the SLM process, rapid melting and solidification are attributable to short-time interaction between laser energy and metal powder, which facilitates the formation of fine microstructure and improves the mechanical properties of the parts []. Meanwhile, ultra-fast cooling helps prevent the formation of intermetallic compounds and element dissolution. Thus, SLM was recently also used for HEA manufacturing, and some studies on the manufacturing, microstructure, and tensile properties of these alloys have been reported []. chosen.conditions: moderate-temperature sinter profile (~1100–1200 °C) in inert or vacuum environment, feedstock as-supplied AlCrFeNiSi powder
chosen.why: Shifting from high-thermal-load fusion-based additive manufacturing to a binder-jetting and sintering route directly tackles both excessive residual thermally induced stress and processing complexity. Binder jetting avoids large thermal gradients during printing and reduces equipment demands relative to fusion processes, thereby minimizing microstructural degradation, improving mechanical performance, and simplifying the fabrication of these miniature AlCrFeNiSi components.
